CALSAVERS RETIREMENT SAVINGS PROGRAM — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

ABOUT THIS CALSAVERS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's CalSavers Retirement Savings Program, established under Government Code § 100000 et seq. (Title 21 of the Government Code, "The CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act," originally enacted as the California Secure Choice Retirement Savings Trust Act), as it relates to Acme Corp., which reports approximately 25 employees in California, and to Jane Doe. It states facts drawn from the statute's own text about what the CalSavers program is, which employers the statute requires to register and by when, the statutory exemption for employers that already sponsor a qualifying retirement plan, the automatic-enrollment and opt-out mechanism available to an eligible employee such as Jane Doe, and the penalty a noncompliant employer may face.

This information sheet does not determine whether Acme Corp. is or is not an "eligible employer" under the statute, whether any plan Acme Corp. offers qualifies for the statutory exemption, whether Acme Corp.'s own registration deadline has already passed, whether Jane Doe is or is not an "eligible employee," or what Acme Corp. or Jane Doe should do about any of the facts it describes.

WHAT THE CALSAVERS PROGRAM IS
The CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust is a trust "administered by the [CalSavers Retirement Savings] board for the purpose of promoting greater retirement savings for California private employees in a convenient, voluntary, low-cost, and portable manner." The CalSavers Retirement Savings Program itself is statutorily defined to "include, as determined by the board, one or more payroll deduction IRA arrangements." A "payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement" is defined as an arrangement by which an employer allows employees to remit payroll-deduction contributions to a retirement savings program, which may include an IRA, and in the case of a payroll deduction IRA arrangement, to remit specifically to an IRA. The statute defines "IRA" to mean an individual retirement account or individual retirement annuity under 26 U.S.C. § 408(a), 408(b), or 408A — the last of which is the Internal Revenue Code section governing Roth IRAs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "There is hereby established a retirement savings trust known as the CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust to be administered by the board for the purpose of promoting greater retirement savings for California private employees in a convenient, voluntary, low-cost, and portable manner."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100004(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, statement of the trust's purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100004.)
  "The CalSavers Retirement Savings Program shall include, as determined by the board, one or more payroll deduction IRA arrangements."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100008 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, definition of the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100008.)
  "(h) “Payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement” means an arrangement by which an employer allows employees to remit payroll deduction contributions to a retirement savings program, which may include an IRA, and in the case of a payroll deduction IRA arrangement, to remit specifically to an IRA."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100000(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, definition of "payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100000.)
  "“IRA” means an individual retirement account or individual retirement annuity under Section 408(a), 408(b), or 408A of Title 26 of the United States Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100000(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, definition of "IRA" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100000.)
  Known gap: The four citations below are all subdivisions or sections of the same statutory title (Government Code, Title 21) rather than independent outside sources: § 100004(a) (trust purpose), § 100008 (program definition), § 100000(h) (payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement definition), and § 100000(e) (IRA definition). The statutory text fetched for this document does not itself state that a Roth IRA (26 U.S.C. § 408A) is the default account type for a CalSavers participant who does not choose otherwise — that default is understood to be set by the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board's implementing regulations (Title 10, California Code of Regulations, Chapter 15, commencing at § 10000), which this document was not able to independently fetch and verify from a primary regulatory source with the same two-fetch discipline used for the Government Code text below. This clause therefore states only that the statute's own "IRA" definition includes the Internal Revenue Code section governing Roth IRAs, and does not itself assert that Roth is the default. This clause also does not cover the program's governance structure (the nine-member CalSavers Retirement Savings Board, § 100002), the trust's fund segregation and investment powers (§ 100004(b)-(f), § 100010), or the separate Retirement Investments Clearinghouse and vendor-registration system (§§ 100016-100030), none of which this document addresses.

WHICH EMPLOYERS MUST REGISTER, AND BY WHEN
The statute phases in the registration requirement by reference to the size of an "eligible employer," measured in "eligible employees," and to the date the CalSavers board opened the program for enrollment. Within 12 months after that date, eligible employers with more than 100 eligible employees, and that do not offer a retirement savings program under subdivision (h), were required to have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement in place. Within 24 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with more than 50 eligible employees. Within 36 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with five or more employees. And "by December 31, 2025," the requirement extended to eligible employers with one or more eligible employees. The board "may extend the time limits" set by these four deadlines "in its discretion."

A statutory "eligible employer" is a business, industry, profession, trade, or other enterprise operating in California — for profit or not for profit — that has at least one eligible employee and satisfies the requirements to establish or participate in a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement; the definition excludes sole proprietorships, self-employed individuals, and other business entities that employ no one but the business's own owners, as well as the federal government, the state, any county, any municipal corporation, and the state's own units or instrumentalities. An "eligible employee" is a person employed by an eligible employer, but the definition excludes an employee covered under the federal Railway Labor Act (or otherwise engaged in interstate commerce beyond the state's legislative power) and an employee for whom an employer makes contributions to a Taft-Hartley pension trust fund — so the count that triggers each deadline is a count of statutorily "eligible" employees, not necessarily an employer's total headcount.

Separately, an employer that already "provides an employer-sponsored retirement plan, such as a defined benefit plan or a 401(k), Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) plan, or Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) plan, or that offers an automatic enrollment payroll deduction IRA," is exempt from the CalSavers registration requirement altogether, provided the plan or IRA "qualifies for favorable federal income tax treatment under the federal Internal Revenue Code," and an employer "retain[s] the option at all times" to set up such a qualifying plan instead of registering for CalSavers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) Within 12 months after the board opens the program for enrollment, eligible employers with more than 100 eligible employees and that do not offer a retirement savings program pursuant to subdivision (h) shall have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement to allow employee participation in the program."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the more-than-100-eligible-employee, 12-month deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(c) Within 24 months after the board opens the program for enrollment, eligible employers with more than 50 eligible employees and that do not offer a retirement savings program pursuant to subdivision (h) shall have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement to allow employee participation in the program."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the more-than-50-eligible-employee, 24-month deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(d) Within 36 months after the board opens the program for enrollment, eligible employers with five or more employees and that do not offer a retirement savings program pursuant to subdivision (h) shall have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement to allow employee participation in the program."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the five-or-more-employee, 36-month deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(e) By December 31, 2025, eligible employers with one or more eligible employees and that do not offer a retirement savings program pursuant to subdivision (h) shall have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement to allow employee participation in the program."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the one-or-more-eligible-employee, December 31, 2025 deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(f) The board, in its discretion, may extend the time limits defined in subdivisions (b) to (e), inclusive."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the board's discretion to extend the deadlines (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(h) (1) An employer that provides an employer-sponsored retirement plan, such as a defined benefit plan or a 401(k), Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) plan, or Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) plan, or that offers an automatic enrollment payroll deduction IRA, shall be exempt from the requirements of the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program, if the plan or IRA qualifies for favorable federal income tax treatment under the federal Internal Revenue Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(h)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the exemption for an employer with a qualifying employer-sponsored plan (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(1) “Eligible employer” means a person or entity engaged in a business, industry, profession, trade, or other enterprise in the state, whether for profit or not for profit, excluding sole proprietorships, self-employed individuals, or other business entities that do not employ any individuals other than the owners of the business, the federal government, the state, any county, any municipal corporation, or any of the state’s units or instrumentalities, that has at least one eligible employee and that satisfies the requirements to establish or participate in a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100000(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, definition of "eligible employer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100000.)
  "(3) “Eligible employer” does not include an employer that provides a retirement savings program as described in subdivision (g) of Section 100032."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100000(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, cross-reference excluding an employer under the (misnumbered) exemption subdivision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100000.)
  "(c) (1) “Eligible employee” means a person who is employed by an eligible employer. (2) “Eligible employee” does not include: (A) Any employee covered under the federal Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. Sec. 151), or any employee engaged in interstate commerce so as not to be subject to the legislative powers of the state, except insofar as application of this title is authorized under the United States Constitution or laws of the United States. (B) Any employee on whose behalf an employer makes contributions to a Taft-Hartley pension trust fund."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100000(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, definition of "eligible employee" and its exclusions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100000.)
  Known gap: Government Code § 100032(b), (c), (d), (e), (f), and (h) are all subdivisions of a single statutory section, not independent sources; § 100000(d)(1) and (d)(3), and § 100000(c), are subdivisions of a separate section (the definitions section) cited here because the deadlines in § 100032 turn on those defined terms. This document independently confirmed a cross-reference discrepancy in the currently codified text: § 100000(d)(3) says an "eligible employer" does not include an employer that provides a qualifying retirement savings program "as described in subdivision (g) of Section 100032," but the actual exemption for an employer-sponsored plan is codified in § 100032, subdivision (h), not subdivision (g) — subdivision (g) of the current text instead governs the automatic-enrollment and opt-out mechanism. This document quotes both provisions exactly as codified and does not resolve or correct the apparent uncorrected cross-reference; it flags the discrepancy rather than assuming which subdivision letter is the "right" one. 

Because today's date is after December 31, 2025, the final phase-in deadline in subdivision (e) has, by its terms, already passed for an eligible employer that was not otherwise exempt — but this document did not independently research whether the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board has since exercised its discretion under subdivision (f) to extend that or any other deadline, and takes no position on whether any particular employer's specific deadline has or has not passed. This clause also does not cover: the date the board actually "opened the program for enrollment" (a factual/historical question this document did not research, since the statute itself does not state that date); the special in-home-supportive-services employer-of-record provisions of § 100046; or § 100043's separate conditions under which the board may operate the program at all (keeping it from being classified as an ERISA plan).

CALSAVERS IS NOT AN EMPLOYER-SPONSORED PLAN
The statute states directly that employers registered for CalSavers are not the plan's sponsor: "Employers shall not be a fiduciary, or considered to be a fiduciary, over the trust or the program. The program is a state-administered program, not an employer-sponsored program. ... An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants." The statute separately provides that "[e]mployers shall not have any liability for an employee's decision to participate in, or opt out of, the program, or for the investment decisions of employees whose assets are deposited in the program." The board is required to disclose the same facts to employees directly: the employee information packet the board designs must state that "[t]his retirement program is not sponsored by the employer, and therefore the employer is not responsible for the plan or liable as a plan sponsor," and that employees seeking financial advice should contact financial advisors rather than their employer, "that employers do not provide financial advice," and "that employees are not to contact their employers for financial advice."

Nothing in the statute requires a registered employer to make any financial contribution to a participating employee's account. A participating employer instead "allow[s]" employee payroll deductions to be remitted to the program; the board's own powers separately include the power to "[a]llow participating employers to make their own contributions to their employees' IRAs," but only if permitted under the Internal Revenue Code and only if doing so would not cause the program to be treated as an employee benefit plan under the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) — describing an option, not a requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

If the program is subsequently found to be preempted by any federal law or regulation, employers shall not be liable as plan sponsors. An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants."
  — Cal. Gov.   — Cal. Gov. Code § 100034(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, employer has no liability for an employee's participation or investment decisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100034.)
  "(c) In addition, the disclosure form shall clearly articulate the following: (1) Employees seeking financial advice should contact financial advisors, that employers do not provide financial advice, that employees are not to contact their employers for financial advice, and that employers are not liable for decisions employees make pursuant to Section 100034. (2) This retirement program is not sponsored by the employer, and therefore the employer is not responsible for the plan or liable as a plan sponsor. (3) The program fund is not guaranteed by the State of California."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100014(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, required employee-disclosure statement that the program is not employer-sponsored (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100014.)
  "(j) Allow participating employers to make their own contributions to their employees’ IRAs, provided that the contributions would be permitted under the Internal Revenue Code and would not cause the program to be treated as an employee benefit plan under the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100012(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, board's power to allow, but not require, voluntary employer contributions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100012.)
  Known gap: § 100034(a) and § 100034(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section; § 100014(c) is a different section (governing the content the board must include in the mandatory employee disclosure form) and § 100012(j) is a different section still (a board power provision), so all four citations below draw from three genuinely distinct sections of the same title, not one source repeated. This clause does not cover § 100034(c) or (d), which address a voluntary employer contribution's effect on the rest of this liability framework and an employer's civil liability for acting under board regulations defining employer roles, or § 100043, which separately conditions the program's operation on the board avoiding ERISA classification in the first place. This document takes no position on whether CalSavers, or an employer's participation in it, is in fact preempted by ERISA or any other federal law — it reports only what the California statute itself says about an employer's liability and fiduciary status.

AUTOMATIC ENROLLMENT, DEFAULT CONTRIBUTION, AND THE OPT-OUT MECHANISM
The statute automatically enrolls an eligible employee of a participating employer: "Each eligible employee shall be enrolled in the program unless the employee elects not to participate in the program. An eligible employee may elect to opt out of the program by making a notation on the opt-out form or by contacting the program by telephone." At least once every two years after the program's initial implementation, the board may designate an open enrollment period in which an employee who previously opted out is again given the disclosure and opt-out forms and may choose to enroll or opt out again. An employee "may also terminate their participation in the program at any time" by the same opt-out mechanisms.

Absent a different election by the employee, "a participating employee shall contribute 3 percent of the employee's annual salary or wages to the program." The board may adjust that default by regulation, but only to somewhere between 2 and 5 percent. The board may also implement annual automatic escalation of a participant's contribution rate, subject to statutory limits: escalated contributions may not exceed 8 percent of salary, and escalation may raise a participant's contribution rate by no more than one percentage point of salary per calendar year; a participant may separately opt out of automatic escalation and set their own contribution percentage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(g) (1) Each eligible employee shall be enrolled in the program unless the employee elects not to participate in the program. An eligible employee may elect to opt out of the program by making a notation on the opt-out form or by contacting the program by telephone."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, automatic enrollment and the opt-out mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(2) Following initial implementation of the program pursuant to this section, at least once every two years, the board may designate an open enrollment period during which eligible employees that previously opted out of the program shall be given the employee information packet with the disclosure and opt-out forms, for the employee to enroll in the program or opt out of the program by making a notation on the opt-out form."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the board's periodic open-enrollment period for employees who previously opted out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(j) Unless otherwise specified by the employee, a participating employee shall contribute 3 percent of the employee’s annual salary or wages to the program."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the default 3% employee contribution rate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(k) By regulation, the board may adjust the contribution amount set in subdivision (j) to no less than 2 percent and no more than 5 percent and may vary that amount within that 2 percent to 5 percent range."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(k) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the board's regulatory power to adjust the default rate between 2% and 5% (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  "(l) The board may implement annual automatic escalation of employee contributions. (1) Employee contributions subject to automatic escalation shall not exceed 8 percent of salary. (2) Automatic escalation shall result in no more than a 1-percent-of-salary increase in employee contributions per calendar year. (3) A participating employee may elect to opt out of automatic escalation and may set their contribution percentage rate at a level determined by the participating employee."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100032(l) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, annual automatic escalation, its 8% cap, and the participant's ability to opt out of escalation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100032.)
  Known gap: § 100032(g)(1), (g)(2), (i), (j), (k), and (l) are all subdivisions of the single statutory section already discussed in this document's coverage-and-deadlines clause, not independent sources — they are treated here as one clause because they together describe a single mechanism (automatic enrollment and its opt-out and contribution-rate features) rather than the separate question of which employers must register. This clause does not cover the content or format the board must give the required disclosure and opt-out forms themselves (§ 100014), the process by which an individual or an employee of a nonparticipating employer may separately enroll and contribute (§ 100012(k)), or any Internal Revenue Code contribution limit that independently caps how much may be contributed to an IRA in a given year regardless of the percentage elected — this document did not research current IRA contribution limits under federal tax law.

PENALTY FOR EMPLOYER NONCOMPLIANCE
The CalSavers Retirement Savings Board has "the power and duties necessary to administer the enforcement of employer compliance with this title." Where an employer fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the program, the board must first issue "a notice of penalty application." A penalty attaches only after a further step: "[e]ach eligible employer that, without good cause, fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program pursuant to Sections 100014 and 100032, after the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board serves a final notice of penalty application, shall be subject to a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per eligible employee and an additional penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per eligible employee if noncompliance continues," as further described in Revenue and Taxation Code § 19287. The Franchise Tax Board, not the CalSavers board itself, issues the actual first notice of penalty imposition once the CalSavers board informs it of an employer's noncompliance, and an eligible employer may appeal any penalty imposed under this section in writing to the Franchise Tax Board under Revenue and Taxation Code § 19288.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) (1) The CalSavers Retirement Savings Board shall issue to each employer who fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the CalSavers Retirement Program pursuant to this title a notice of penalty application."
  — Cal. Gov.   "(2) Each eligible employer that, without good cause, fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program pursuant to Sections 100014 and 100032, after the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board serves a final notice of penalty application, shall be subject to a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per eligible employee and an additional penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per eligible employee if noncompliance continues as described in Section 19287 of the Revenue and Taxation Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 100033(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act, the $250-per-employee and additional $500-per-employee penalty amounts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=100033.)
  Known gap: § 100033(a), (b)(1), (b)(2), (c), and (d) are subdivisions of a single statutory section. This clause quotes the Government Code's own cross-references to Revenue and Taxation Code §§ 19287 and 19288 (the statutes actually governing the Franchise Tax Board's notice and appeal procedure and any further mechanics of penalty calculation) but did not independently fetch and verify the text of either Revenue and Taxation Code section with the same two-fetch discipline used for the Government Code text above — a real limitation in this document's research, disclosed rather than papered over. This clause also does not state what "good cause" means (the phrase is used but not defined anywhere in the Title 21 text this document reviewed), does not address whether the $250/$500 per-employee penalty figures have been adjusted since last amended, and does not cover any other consequence of noncompliance that might exist outside this statute.

This clause also does not cover the program's governance structure (the nine-member CalSavers Retirement Savings Board, § 100002), the trust's fund segregation and investment powers (§ 100004(b)-(f), § 100010), or the separate Retirement Investments Clearinghouse and vendor-registration system (§§ 100016-100030), none of which this document addresses.

expectedJSON.body:
The statute phases in the registration requirement by reference to the size of an "eligible employer," measured in "eligible employees," and to the date the CalSavers board opened the program for enrollment. Within 12 months after that date, eligible employers with more than 100 eligible employees, and that do not offer a retirement savings program under subdivision (h), were required to have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement in place. Within 24 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with more than 50 eligible employees. Within 36 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with five or more employees. And "by December 31, 2025," the requirement extended to eligible employers with one or more eligible employees. The board "may extend the time limits" set by these four deadlines "in its discretion."

A statutory "eligible employer" is a business, industry, profession, trade, or other enterprise operating in California — for profit or not for profit — that has at least one eligible employee and satisfies the requirements to establish or participate in a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement; the definition excludes sole proprietorships, self-employed individuals, and other business entities that employ no one but the business's own owners, as well as the federal government, the state, any county, any municipal corporation, and the state's own units or instrumentalities. An "eligible employee" is a person employed by an eligible employer, but the definition excludes an employee covered under the federal Railway Labor Act (or otherwise engaged in interstate commerce beyond the state's legislative power) and an employee for whom an employer makes contributions to a Taft-Hartley pension trust fund — so the count that triggers each deadline is a count of statutorily "eligible" employees, not necessarily an employer's total headcount.

Separately, an employer that already "provides an employer-sponsored retirement plan, such as a defined benefit plan or a 401(k), Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) plan, or Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) plan, or that offers an automatic enrollment payroll deduction IRA," is exempt from the CalSavers registration requirement altogether, provided the plan or IRA "qualifies for favorable federal income tax treatment under the federal Internal Revenue Code," and an employer "retain[s] the option at all times" to set up such a qualifying plan instead of registering for CalSavers.

expectedJSON.body:
The statute states directly that employers registered for CalSavers are not the plan's sponsor: "Employers shall not be a fiduciary, or considered to be a fiduciary, over the trust or the program. The program is a state-administered program, not an employer-sponsored program. ... An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants." The statute separately provides that "[e]mployers shall not have any liability for an employee's decision to participate in, or opt out of, the program, or for the investment decisions of employees whose assets are deposited in the program." The board is required to disclose the same facts to employees directly: the employee information packet the board designs must state that "[t]his retirement program is not sponsored by the employer, and therefore the employer is not responsible for the plan or liable as a plan sponsor," and that employees seeking financial advice should contact financial advisors rather than their employer, "that employers do not provide financial advice," and "that employees are not to contact their employers for financial advice."

Nothing in the statute requires a registered employer to make any financial contribution to a participating employee's account. A participating employer instead "allow[s]" employee payroll deductions to be remitted to the program; the board's own powers separately include the power to "[a]llow participating employers to make their own contributions to their employees' IRAs," but only if permitted under the Internal Revenue Code and only if doing so would not cause the program to be treated as an employee benefit plan under the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) — describing an option, not a requirement.

The program is a state-administered program, not an employer-sponsored program. If the program is subsequently found to be preempted by any federal law or regulation, employers shall not be liable as plan sponsors. An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants.

expectedJSON.body:
The statute automatically enrolls an eligible employee of a participating employer: "Each eligible employee shall be enrolled in the program unless the employee elects not to participate in the program. An eligible employee may elect to opt out of the program by making a notation on the opt-out form or by contacting the program by telephone." At least once every two years after the program's initial implementation, the board may designate an open enrollment period in which an employee who previously opted out is again given the disclosure and opt-out forms and may choose to enroll or opt out again. An employee "may also terminate their participation in the program at any time" by the same opt-out mechanisms.

Absent a different election by the employee, "a participating employee shall contribute 3 percent of the employee's annual salary or wages to the program." The board may adjust that default by regulation, but only to somewhere between 2 and 5 percent. The board may also implement annual automatic escalation of a participant's contribution rate, subject to statutory limits: escalated contributions may not exceed 8 percent of salary, and escalation may raise a participant's contribution rate by no more than one percentage point of salary per calendar year; a participant may separately opt out of automatic escalation and set their own contribution percentage.

expectedJSON.body: The CalSavers Retirement Savings Board has "the power and duties necessary to administer the enforcement of employer compliance with this title." Where an employer fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the program, the board must first issue "a notice of penalty application." A penalty attaches only after a further step: "[e]ach eligible employer that, without good cause, fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program pursuant to Sections 100014 and 100032, after the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board serves a final notice of penalty application, shall be subject to a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per eligible employee and an additional penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per eligible employee if noncompliance continues," as further described in Revenue and Taxation Code § 19287. The Franchise Tax Board, not the CalSavers board itself, issues the actual first notice of penalty imposition once the CalSavers board informs it of an employer's noncompliance, and an eligible employer may appeal any penalty imposed under this section in writing to the Franchise Tax Board under Revenue and Taxation Code § 19288.

This clause quotes the Government Code's own cross-references to Revenue and Taxation Code §§ 19287 and 19288 (the statutes actually governing the Franchise Tax Board's notice and appeal procedure and any further mechanics of penalty calculation) but did not independently fetch and verify the text of either Revenue and Taxation Code section with the same two-fetch discipline used for the Government Code text above — a real limitation in this document's research, disclosed rather than papered over. This clause also does not state what "good cause" means (the phrase is used but not defined anywhere in the Title 21 text this document reviewed), does not address whether the $250/$500 per-employee penalty figures have been adjusted since last amended, and does not cover any other consequence of noncompliance that might exist outside this statute.
